question: Generate a hierarchical clustering heatmap to visualize metabolic differences among tissue samples. Z-score standardize the metabolite intensities, then produce a clustermap with a tissue-type color sidebar derived from the sample metadata.

files.eval_guideline: Clustermap must show hierarchical clustering dendrograms with z-scored cell values and a tissue-type color sidebar; color palette and dendrogram aesthetics may differ.
files.match_reasoning: Both files are named clustermap.png and are PNG images, which is the clustermap heatmap the task asks for.
files.strategy_reasoning: The output is a PNG image. The guideline asks for visual features (dendrograms, z-scored values, a tissue-type color sidebar) and lets aesthetics differ, so a semantic comparison fits best.

comparison_details.explanation:
Both images are hierarchical-clustering clustermaps of the same tissue-metabolomics dataset (DIAG-160xx/161xx samples, about 555 metabolites). Each has dendrograms on both axes, z-scored cell values and a two-category tissue-type color sidebar. The reference puts samples on rows (blue/orange TISSUE_TYPE sidebar, z-score scale about -2 to 7). The candidate is transposed, with samples on columns (red TUMOR / blue NORMAL bar with a legend, z-scores of log2 intensity capped at ±3).

After accounting for the swapped axes and the different colors, the sample clustering structure largely matches.
- A small separate cluster contains DIAG-16108, 16122, 16130 and 16132. The candidate adds 16096, 16118 and 16112. In both figures this cluster has the same tissue label as the large final cluster (blue in the reference, TUMOR in the candidate).
- A solid block of the other tissue type follows (orange in the reference, NORMAL in the candidate). It includes 16101, 16093, 16117, 16091, 16129, 16105, 16125, 16131, 16099, 16083, 16077 and 16135.
- A large mostly-tumor block follows, with a few samples of the other tissue type mixed in near 16127, 16103/16115 and 16078/16082.

Both figures therefore convey the same message: metabolic profiles largely separate tumor from normal tissue, with a small distinct tumor subgroup and a few misclustered samples.

The differences come from preprocessing (the candidate log2-transforms the data and caps the color scale; the reference has a constant grey column and a wider z-range) and from small changes in sample positions (for example, 16079 is in the normal block in the candidate but at the bottom of the mixed group in the reference). The guideline allows the aesthetic differences. All required elements are present.
